blocks.text: A 20-week ultrasound reports an anterior placenta with its lower edge 15 mm from the internal cervical os. Interpret this finding and discuss the next step.
A 32-week pregnant woman presents with painless vaginal bleeding. Ultrasound demonstrates a placenta covering the internal cervical os. What is your diagnosis and how would you manage her?
A woman has been told that she has a low-lying placenta at her anomaly scan. Explain what this means.
You are shown an obstetric ultrasound. Identify the placental location and state its significance.
Placental localisation means determining:

items: Its relationship to the internal cervical os
Whether there are features suggesting abnormal placental invasion

blocks.text: The placenta may be:
Anterior or posterior placenta alone is not abnormal.
The important question is:
Where is the lower placental edge in relation to the internal cervical os?
The internal cervical os is the internal opening of the cervix into the uterine cavity.
When assessing a low placenta, determine:
Distance between the placental edge and the internal cervical os.
This is clinically important because a placenta close to or covering the cervix may interfere with vaginal delivery and is associated with antepartum haemorrhage.
Placenta praevia refers to a placenta that:
Overlies the internal cervical os.
This is a major cause of:
Antepartum haemorrhage.
Painless, bright-red vaginal bleeding in the second half of pregnancy.
This distinction is extremely important.
Placenta covers/overlies the internal cervical os.
Placental edge is close to the internal cervical os but does not cover it.
Use the terminology and distance threshold specified by your local guideline/exam system.

subsections.subsection_title: Why does the placenta sometimes appear low early in pregnancy?

blocks.text: Because as the uterus enlarges during pregnancy:

items: The relationship between the placenta and cervix changes

blocks.text: Therefore:
A low placenta identified at the mid-trimester scan does not necessarily remain low at term.
This is sometimes described as:
Strictly speaking, the placenta does not actively crawl upward; rather, the uterus changes shape and the placental relationship to the internal os changes.

subsections.subsection_title: What should you tell a woman with a low-lying placenta?

blocks.text: A good explanation:

"The placenta is currently positioned close to the opening of the cervix. This is relatively common when identified at the mid-pregnancy scan, and in many women the placenta is no longer close to the cervix later in pregnancy as the uterus grows. We will arrange follow-up imaging to reassess its position."
Then explain:
"If it remains very close to or covers the cervix later in pregnancy, it may affect the safest mode of delivery and can increase the risk of bleeding."
A woman with a low-lying placenta identified at the mid-trimester scan generally requires:
Follow-up ultrasound later in pregnancy.
The exact timing depends on:
This is an important OSCE point.
If precise placental localisation is required:
Transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS) can provide an accurate assessment of the relationship between the placental edge and internal cervical os.

content_groups.group_title: Is TVUS safe in placenta praevia?

blocks.text: Yes, when appropriately performed by trained personnel.
It is not the same thing as a digital vaginal examination.
This is a critical safety issue.
If placenta praevia is suspected in a woman with antepartum bleeding:
Do not perform a digital vaginal examination until placenta praevia has been excluded.
Why?
Because digital examination can potentially disturb the placenta and cause:
Severe haemorrhage.

with:
Digital vaginal examination.

Soft and non-tender.

subsections.subsection_title: Why is previous caesarean section important?

blocks.text: A previous caesarean scar is associated with:
Increased risk of placenta praevia.
Increased risk of placenta accreta spectrum when placenta is implanted over/near the scar.
Therefore:
Placenta praevia + previous caesarean section = think placenta accreta spectrum.
This is a very high-yield association.
This refers to abnormal placental adherence/invasion.
The spectrum includes:
Placenta abnormally adherent to the myometrium.
Placental villi invade:
Into the myometrium.
Placental tissue penetrates through the myometrium and may involve surrounding structures.

subsections.subsection_title: What if placenta accreta is suspected?

blocks.text: This is not a routine antenatal issue.
Management should involve:

items: Delivery planning in an appropriately equipped centre

blocks.text: Potential complications include:
Massive obstetric haemorrhage.

items: "Does this mean I cannot have a vaginal delivery?"

blocks.text: "Not necessarily. A placenta that is low at the mid-trimester scan may move away from the cervix as the uterus grows. We will reassess its position later in pregnancy. If it remains over or very close to the cervix, we will discuss the safest mode of delivery based on the final ultrasound findings and your clinical circumstances."
"No. Placental location is not something you caused. There are certain factors that increase the likelihood, but it is not generally something a woman has done to cause."
Better terminology:

"The placenta itself does not actively move. As the uterus grows and the lower uterine segment develops, the relationship between the placenta and the cervix often changes, so the placenta may no longer be close to the cervical opening later in pregnancy."
Excellent OSCE answer.

subsections.subsection_title: If the placenta is low but not covering the os

blocks.text: This is more nuanced.
The decision depends on:

items: Exact distance from the internal os

blocks.text: Therefore don't automatically say:
"A woman at 37 weeks has placenta praevia covering the cervix but is not bleeding. What would you do?"

"This represents persistent placenta praevia. I would confirm the placental location and review the antenatal plan. Since the placenta covers the internal cervical os, vaginal delivery would not be appropriate. I would arrange planned caesarean delivery at the recommended gestational age according to local guideline, with appropriate preparation for potential haemorrhage."
"A woman at 22 weeks has an anterior placenta 10 mm from the internal os. What would you do?"

"I would explain that the placenta is low lying at this stage and that the finding does not necessarily persist until term. I would arrange follow-up ultrasound, preferably with accurate assessment of the relationship between the placental edge and internal cervical os, and counsel her regarding symptoms requiring urgent assessment, particularly vaginal bleeding."

content_groups.group_title: Q2. What is the classic presentation?

blocks.text: Painless vaginal bleeding in the second half of pregnancy, often bright red.

content_groups.group_title: Q3. What is the difference between placenta praevia and low-lying placenta?

blocks.text: Placenta praevia overlies the internal cervical os, while a low-lying placenta is close to but does not cover the internal os.
Q4. What is the safest ultrasound method for accurately assessing placental relationship to the cervix?
Transvaginal ultrasound, when indicated and performed appropriately.

content_groups.group_title: Q5. Is transvaginal ultrasound contraindicated in placenta praevia?

blocks.text: No. It can be safely performed when clinically indicated by an appropriately trained clinician.

content_groups.group_title: Q6. Can you perform a digital vaginal examination in suspected placenta praevia?

blocks.text: Not until placenta praevia has been excluded, because examination may precipitate severe haemorrhage.

content_groups.group_title: Q7. What is the classic presentation of abruption?

blocks.text: Painful vaginal bleeding, uterine tenderness/irritability and possible fetal compromise.

content_groups.group_title: Q8. What is the major risk of placenta praevia?

blocks.text: Major obstetric haemorrhage.
Q9. What major complication should you consider when placenta praevia occurs over a previous caesarean scar?
Placenta accreta spectrum.
Placental villi invade into the myometrium.
Placental tissue penetrates through the myometrium and may invade surrounding organs.

content_groups.group_title: Q12. What is the management if placenta praevia persists over the cervical os?

blocks.text: Planned caesarean delivery, with timing determined by guideline and clinical circumstances.
Saying:
It isn't.
Calling every low placenta:
Not necessarily.
You need to know its relationship to the internal os.
Performing a digital vaginal examination in suspected placenta praevia.
Dangerous.
Forgetting placenta accreta when there is:
Previous caesarean + anterior low placenta.
Telling every woman with a low placenta that she will definitely need a caesarean.
The placental position may change as pregnancy progresses.
Forgetting maternal resuscitation in major bleeding.
Always think:
Mother first → fetus → definitive obstetric management.
"The placenta is posterior and appears appropriately located, with the lower placental edge clear of the internal cervical os."

"The placenta is posterior and low lying, with the lower placental edge close to the internal cervical os. I would correlate with the formal measurement and arrange follow-up imaging according to guideline."
"The placenta overlies the internal cervical os, consistent with placenta praevia."

"There is an anterior low-lying placenta in a woman with previous caesarean delivery, with sonographic features concerning for placenta accreta spectrum. This requires specialist fetal medicine assessment and multidisciplinary delivery planning."
And:
Previous CS + anterior low placenta = ACCRETA until properly assessed.
"A woman with known placenta praevia presents with vaginal bleeding. What is the first thing you do?"
Don't start with ultrasound.
Don't start with a vaginal examination.
Your answer should begin:

"I would assess and stabilise the mother using an ABCDE approach, quantify the bleeding, establish IV access, send appropriate blood tests and crossmatch blood, assess fetal wellbeing, and involve the senior obstetric, anaesthetic and neonatal teams as appropriate. I would avoid digital vaginal examination until placenta praevia has been excluded."
That demonstrates safe obstetric practice, which is exactly what the examiner is looking for.
